passage: When the ordering system in the Lisbon office went dark at ten past two, the chat filled with people typing at once. Beatriz wrote, 'I'll be incident commander. Olga, you investigate. Mateus, you talk to customers and management.' Then she asked everyone else to stay quiet in the main thread unless called on. Olga opened the logs and posted findings every ten minutes. Mateus sent a short note to the support desk and another to the director, and promised the next one at three. Beatriz kept a running list of what had been tried. Nobody dug through the same log twice, and nobody talked over anyone. At ten to four the fix went in and the system came back. Beatriz thanked each role by name and set a review for the next morning.

qa.q: Who did Beatriz tell to investigate?
What did Beatriz want when she asked everyone else to stay quiet in the main thread?
qa.a: Beatriz wanted calm and focus, so that the investigator and the person sending updates could work without being talked over.

qa.q: What could the team add if an outage ran for many hours?
qa.a: The team could rotate the roles after some hours so people stay rested, using the running list to hand over.

qa.q: How might the director have felt about Mateus's updates?
qa.a: The director would probably feel informed and calmer, since the notes came when promised.

grounding: Shows a team naming one incident commander, one investigator and one person who updates customers and management.

passage:
The status board in the operations room turned red at 2.30 p.m.: the booking site was down. Six engineers crowded round Jagdish's desk, all talking.
Jagdish stood up. 'Stop. Roles first.' He pointed. 'I'm incident commander. I don't touch code; I decide and keep time. Farhan, you investigate. You only talk to me. Neha, you update customers and management every twenty minutes. Nobody else messages the CEO. Everyone else, stay in the channel and wait for Farhan to ask.'
The noise dropped. Farhan found a full disk on the booking server in twelve minutes and said so once, clearly. Jagdish approved the cleanup. Neha posted: 'Cause found, fix in progress, next update 3.10.'
The site was back at 2.58. Nobody had shouted over anyone else.

qa.q: Who did Jagdish ask to update customers and management?
What does the room's noise dropping suggest the engineers felt?
qa.a: It suggests they felt relieved and calmer once each person knew their role.

qa.q: What else could the team do to make the roles automatic next time?
qa.a: They could write the three roles into a short incident guide and practise it, so no one has to organise the room on the spot.

qa.q: How might management experience this incident?
qa.a: Management got clear updates every twenty minutes from one person, instead of confusing messages from many.

grounding: It shows a team naming one incident commander, one investigator and one person to update customers and management so people do not duplicate work.

passage:
Hi Uma,
Welcome to the team. Since you'll be on the on-call rota from next month, here's the one thing I wish someone had told me in my first week.
Last March, the search service went down, and eight of us jumped on it at once. Two people restarted the same server. Three people messaged the director with different stories. Nobody told customers anything for an hour.
Since then we always name three roles in the first five minutes. One incident commander, who decides and doesn't debug. One investigator, who finds the cause. One communicator, who updates customers and management on a fixed schedule. Everyone else waits to be asked.
The first time I was commander, my hands were itching to fix things myself. Don't. Just keep the room calm.
See you at Thursday's drill,
Farhan

qa.q: How many people jumped on the search outage last March?
qa.a: Eight of them jumped on it at once.

qa.q: How did Farhan feel the first time as commander?
qa.a: Farhan felt restless and tempted to fix things personally, hands itching to debug.

qa.q: What could Uma do to prepare before joining the rota?
qa.a: Uma could join the Thursday drill and practise each role once, so the roles feel familiar before a real outage.

qa.q: How were customers affected before the team used roles?
qa.a: Nobody told them anything for an hour, leaving them confused while eight people worked on the problem.

grounding: It shows the value of naming an incident commander, an investigator and a communicator so people don't duplicate work or talk over each other.
